name: Surfer hair

card.summary: A medium-to-long, layered, tousled hairstyle with a beachy wave that gives a relaxed, casual look with minimal styling.

quick.overview:
Surfer hair is a medium to long, layered style with textured ends and loose waves, often sun-lightened. It is meant to look natural and windswept rather than groomed.

It grew out of California surf culture in the 1950s and 1960s, and is now a common casual look. No clinical research addresses it.
quick.how: People grow out layers and style with sea-salt spray, texturising products and air-drying, with occasional trims. It suits straight, wavy and curly textures.
quick.risks: No health risks; frequent salt sprays and sun may dry hair, and the look needs enough hair density and length to carry.

lead: Surfer hair is a medium-to-long layered hairstyle with choppy ends and loose waves, aiming for a relaxed windswept look. According to Grokipedia, it originated in 1950s and 1960s Southern California surf culture.[1]

People use it to soften the face, add texture and frame the forehead and cheeks. Popular culture of the era helped spread it, including the 1959 film Gidget and Bruce Brown's 1966 documentary The Endless Summer, per that source.[1]

angle.text: The layers and waves add volume and movement and soften the face outline, which people use for an easy, outdoorsy look.

paras: The style is layered with textured ends and loose waves, often with sun-lightened strands.[1]
Grokipedia traces it to surf culture in Malibu and San Onofre in the 1950s, and says it spread to wider fashion and countercultural scenes through the 1960s and 1970s.[1]
